title: Exploring AI-Powered Litigation with FileRead's Chan Koh and Justin Brownstone
author: Chan-Hee Koh · Justin Brownstone

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source predicts that AI may reach junior-associate capability and significantly alter law-firm structure and operations, which is compatible with automation displacing junior work. However, it does not address whether this would impair expertise reproduction, create a verification paradox, or require reconstructed apprenticeship through simulation, mentorship and independent practice.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led work-redesign proposition and develops it through a concrete litigation workflow: AI handles large-scale document search, chronology and fact development so attorneys can focus on targeted analysis and strategy. It also endorses selective, client-informed deployment rather than feature-led adoption, although its performance claims rest mainly on vendor anecdotes rather than independent evaluation.
qs: And so I think how do we get them to do more of the strategic things, the more creative things that really add value for the people that actually need their legal services rather than the things that think our machines frankly can do a lot better now that the technology has gotten to this point.

So really trying to hone in on that, talk to more people, talk to as many people as possible, really understand which part of the process can we add the most value and just focusing on those and then continuing to build a more comprehensive product suite that encompasses the entire litigation cycle.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account of agentic AI as a shift from point solutions toward planning and orchestrating connected, multi-step legal work. It applies that rationale to document review and brief writing and anticipates attorney augmentation, but provides no measured performance evidence and does not address the cluster’s central concerns about error propagation, verification bottlenecks or governance.
qs: And so that sounds very nice in assuming it’s true, but I think these types of tools, we’re starting to kind of go from a functional, like a point solution that solves a very specific problem to more of like an agentic type of thing where the model itself can start to plan things, make decisions, and then call different functions that it needs to.
And so these tools are actually perfect to help, these tools are now perfect to help orchestrate those type of tasks so that you can do that, so that attorneys can actually do those types of work.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that agentic AI creates value by orchestrating connected legal tasks rather than providing isolated answers, and frames it as augmenting attorneys. Its support is limited and prospective: it offers litigation examples and internal experimentation but does not substantively address tacit expertise, client context, evaluation, verification checkpoints or measured reliability.
qs: Because when you’re doing document review or doing like, if you’re writing a brief, you’re not just doing one thing, you’re doing multiple things all at once.
And so these tools are actually perfect to help, these tools are now perfect to help orchestrate those type of tasks so that you can do that, so that attorneys can actually do those types of work.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that providing AI tools is insufficient: education, guidance and effective, value-adding human use are necessary to turn technology into practical advantage. It does not substantively address renewal economics, consumption pricing or platform control, so it supports rather than materially extends the broader synthesis.
qs: especially in this space of, as you see with like rapid growth, we want to also be play a part in educating the industry, not just providing tools and extracting value from the industry.
They’re going to always trust the people that  have used these tools and use it in a way that they can understand and they can add value.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on selective, practical learning rather than indiscriminately pursuing every release. Koh describes ongoing experimentation but prioritises user-informed litigation value and warns against novel features that amount to low-value “party tricks”; the evidence remains experiential rather than measured.

kp.k: Litigation uncertainty drives costs and motivates AI fact development
kp.d: Koh argues that inaccessible legal services reflect uncertainty about the work needed for resolution, rather than simply arbitrary pricing. He positions FileRead's litigation and e-discovery focus as a way to find relevant facts and unknown issues faster. This is his explanation of the problem and product purpose, not evidence of demonstrated improvements in access to justice.
qs: the main reason why I think legal services are out of reach for a lot of those people is not because of just arbitrary prices, but more due to the uncertainty of the work that needs to be done in order to find a resolution.

what FileRead is really aimed at is helping address this core part of that litigation process by helping litigation professionals find the facts that matter faster, but also uncover the hidden stories in their data.

kp.k: AI promises earlier analysis of massive document productions
kp.d: Brownstone contrasts his recollection of reviewing perhaps five million documents in the Washington Mutual bankruptcy in 2009 with FileRead's ability to answer factual questions and generate memoranda and chronologies within Relativity. He recalls six months of first-level review at 60 hours a week; this personal experience illustrates the workflow problem, rather than establishing measured AI time savings.
qs: JP Morgan dumped, I can’t remember, maybe five million documents on us.
I spent the first six months of my legal career just clicking not relevant for 60 hours a week.
instead of spending six months to do first level review and then start to build chronologies, figure out if there are hot docs, you can ask immediately, tell me if this information is in here.

kp.k: Uncertain litigation workflows complicate technology adoption
kp.d: Koh says his technology-sector experience initially highlighted slower legal adoption, but litigation's uncertain outcomes, document volumes and evolving arguments helped him understand existing practices. His proposed response is technology that exposes unknowns and tests factual propositions, rather than treating litigation as a predictable product-development process.
qs: I have a product background, come from a tech background and the adoption curve there is much steeper than what we see in legal.
But in litigation, outcomes aren’t necessarily guaranteed.
you might find something else that potentially just derails the entire line of thinking that you initially had.

kp.k: Automation should redirect lawyers toward strategy and creativity
kp.d: Koh advocates shifting lawyers away from prolonged document inspection toward strategic and creative work that benefits clients, asserting that machines can now perform some document-intensive tasks better. This is an augmentation-oriented recommendation, not a reported staffing reduction or quantified productivity result.
qs: no one wants to be stuck in a room looking through documents like 10 hours a day.

how do we get them to do more of the strategic things, the more creative things that really add value for the people that actually need their legal services rather than the things that think our machines frankly can do a lot better now that the technology has gotten to this point.

kp.k: Roadmap extends beyond Relativity into automated litigation workflows
kp.d: Brownstone describes a planned standalone analysis platform, explicitly not an e-discovery platform, expected hopefully within a month of the interview. For the rest of 2025, planned extraction capabilities would underpin automated checks of whether documents support allegations, depositions, discovery responses and pleadings. He distinguishes existing allegation-by-allegation questioning from planned automation and anticipates a Q3/Q4 adoption push targeting large litigation departments.
qs: the biggest focus right now is releasing our own standalone platform, which won’t be eDiscovery platform to be clear.
hopefully within a month, you’ll be able to do that outside Relativity.
So you could take the tool and you could one by one ask is this allegation supported? Is this allegation supported? We want to automate that
we think we’ll have a really big push Q3, Q4 to get large litigation departments to adopt FileRead.

kp.k: Integration, citation support and price differentiate the vendor
kp.d: Brownstone claims FileRead is then the only native Relativity option for this type of analysis, while acknowledging competitors may emerge. He also claims accurate work product across millions of documents through multiple models, including a proprietary citation model linking memorandum content to supporting documents, and competitive pricing. These are vendor claims; the discussion supplies no comparative test results, accuracy measurements or prices.
qs: if you want to do it directly within Relativity, we’re a native application within Relativity we’re your your only option.
We use several models, including our own citations model that we built so that we tie everything within a memo to a document for support.
And that is very accurate over large volumes, millions of documents.
I think we need to be competitive on price

kp.d: Koh identifies associates conducting factual analysis after first-level review as particularly suitable users, though use spans multiple roles. He recounts unnamed matters in which a document initially marked not hot became an exhibit after factual development, and in which identifying a person referenced only by first name helped lawyers consider further document requests. These are vendor-reported use cases without case identifiers or systematic outcome data.

there was this one document that was marked not hot in first level review
they ended up promoting that document to an exhibit.
if someone’s reference or CC it on a communication, just using their first name, FileRead was actually able to give them a way to quickly verify who that person was

kp.d: Koh expects increasingly commoditized large language models to enable many new functionalities. He identifies prioritization as the challenge: avoid impressive but low-value demonstrations, consult users about their needs, and build a more comprehensive litigation product suite around valuable workflow problems.

making sure that we stay focused and don’t get distracted on the other cool things that look promising, but potentially it just be like a, almost like a party trick and not really add a lot of value.

kp.d: Brownstone contrasts earlier legal-AI enthusiasm with his impression that current large language models are fundamentally changing practice. Referring to Bob Ambrogi's comparison of legal research tools, he judges the technology not yet equivalent to desired junior-associate work but likely to improve. He predicts substantial changes in firm structure and operations without specifying staffing ratios, displacement numbers or timing.

These are development directions and expected benefits, not demonstrated deployment outcomes.

kp.d: Koh describes ongoing client collaboration and CLE programs as ways to guide adoption amid rapid technological change and knowledge-worker anxiety. He recommends developing distinctive ways to use AI rather than merely chasing each new tool, arguing that trust will remain attached to people who use technology effectively.
qs: We also offer CLE programs with our clients as well.
we want to also be play a part in educating the industry, not just providing tools and extracting value from the industry.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Koh presents faster AI-assisted fact discovery as a way to reduce litigation uncertainty, which he identifies as a reason legal services are inaccessible.
pts.d: At 06:05 and 13:02–15:00, Chan-Hee Koh describes FileRead's aim as finding relevant facts and hidden narratives faster, identifying unknowns and validating case theories. He links this aim to his parents' experience losing their home and not knowing how to obtain legal help. This is a rationale and intended contribution to access, not a claim that FileRead has already reduced the justice gap or client prices.

pts.k: Brownstone claims AI enables immediate questioning and work-product generation over litigation documents rather than waiting through lengthy initial review.
pts.d: At 08:08, Justin Brownstone contrasts FileRead's Relativity-based search, chronology and fact-memo functions with his own first six months as a lawyer doing relevance review. He also describes a longer-term vision of managing litigation facts beyond e-discovery. At 15:00, Koh argues that machines can now do repetitive document work better, allowing lawyers to concentrate on strategic and creative work. The framing is lawyer augmentation; neither speaker quantifies job displacement or establishes an end-to-end replacement for all review.

pts.k: Brownstone claims FileRead combines native Relativity access, accurate large-volume work product and competitive pricing.
pts.d: At 19:07, Brownstone says FileRead is currently the only native Relativity option for this type of work. He attributes accuracy over millions of documents to multiple models, including a proprietary citations model linking memo content to supporting documents. He also presents cost-effectiveness as a differentiator. These are vendor claims about functionality and market position, not independent comparative findings. Linking output to documents is described as a technical support mechanism; no human verification procedure or measured error rate is supplied.

pts.k: Koh reports that AI-assisted factual development can recover overlooked important documents and identify additional sources of evidence.
pts.d: At 20:46, Koh describes an unnamed litigation in which a document initially marked not hot was identified as relevant as the factual narrative developed and was promoted to an exhibit. He also describes targeted searches during deposition preparation and identifying a person referred to by first name so a team could decide whether to request that person's documents. These examples concern substantive fact development and discovery decisions, rather than only faster document classification.

pts.k: Brownstone forecasts a standalone platform and automated litigation workflows that check allegations against underlying evidence.
pts.d: At 16:19, Brownstone outlines a 2025 roadmap: make existing analysis available without requiring documents to reside in Relativity, develop extraction from pleadings and other legal documents, and then automate checking support for factual assertions across complaints, depositions, discovery responses and pleadings. He distinguishes the planned standalone analysis platform from an e-discovery platform. He says individual allegation checks are already possible through repeated questions; the planned change is workflow automation.

pts.k: Brownstone predicts improving language models will reach junior-associate-like research capability and force significant changes in law-firm structure and operations.
pts.d: At 18:25, Brownstone argues that technology now enables useful litigation tools where contractual analysis had previously been easier to automate. At 23:49, he contrasts earlier AI enthusiasm with what he sees as current fundamental change. He treats junior-associate-level research as a likely future development, not an already achieved result. He does not specify a staffing shape, reductions in headcount, leverage changes or a billing-model outcome.

pts.k: Koh predicts commoditized models and agentic orchestration will enable broader litigation applications and improve lawyers' multi-step work.
pts.d: At 22:33, Koh expects increasingly commoditized language models to support more functionality, while making selection of genuinely valuable workflows a central product challenge. At 25:24, he describes a transition from point solutions to systems that plan, make decisions and call functions. He sees these systems as capable of coordinating document-review and brief-writing tasks so attorneys can work faster, more effectively and explore additional inquiries under deadlines. He describes internal experimentation and incorporation, not a demonstrated fully autonomous litigation service. He also predicts that application builders translating model capabilities into practical value will be the ultimate winners.

pts.k: Koh argues that effective AI adoption can create professional competitive advantage while trust remains centered on people.
pts.d: At 27:54, Koh recommends adopting tools and developing distinctive ways of using them rather than focusing on each new release. He presents customer partnership and continuing legal education as ways to help practitioners navigate rapid change. His claim is that trusted professionals who can explain and deliver value through AI remain important; it is not a claim that software alone replaces client relationships.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers vendor experience, unnamed customer anecdotes, personal professional experience and an external review reference, rather than formal performance data.
pts.d: Koh's access rationale draws on his family's housing-loss experience and his interpretation of litigation uncertainty. Brownstone's review comparison draws on his 2009 practice experience; he expressly qualifies the remembered document count. Koh supplies concrete but unnamed customer examples of finding a useful document and identifying a person. Brownstone supplies an architectural explanation for accuracy but no benchmark, accuracy percentage, comparison protocol, pricing figures or measured savings. His junior-associate prediction is informed by his reading of a Bob Ambrogi comparison of legal research tools, not by a reported controlled evaluation. Koh's agentic claims draw on internal experimentation; he also acknowledges poor personal results with deep research. His secondhand molecular-research story is explicitly uncertain and is not evidence of legal performance. Broad market, firm-structure and trust predictions are judgments, not quantified findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current functionality is distinguished from a sequenced 2025 roadmap and open-ended predictions about professional change.
pts.d: At interview time, Brownstone describes FileRead analysis as available natively within Relativity, with exclusivity expressly qualified by the possibility of competitors entering. The standalone platform is hoped for within a month; extraction precedes later-2025 automated workflows, followed by a planned Q3/Q4 adoption push. These are prospective commitments, not confirmed releases. The broader litigation-suite vision, junior-associate capability prediction, structural changes to firms and agentic opportunities have no precise completion date; some arise in a discussion of the next few years. Koh conditions valuable product expansion on customer needs and prioritization rather than novelty. He also emphasizes that litigation outcomes remain uncertain even with better fact discovery.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected users are litigation associates and teams handling large document sets; broader claimed effects reach firms, clients and legal-AI application builders.
pts.d: Koh identifies attorneys, particularly associates developing facts after first-level review, as the best-fit users, while acknowledging a broader user base that includes litigation support. Relativity users are the immediate market; the standalone roadmap would remove that platform prerequisite. Large litigation departments are a stated adoption target, without a clear distinction between law-firm and corporate departments. Claimed benefits include faster targeted searches, stronger deposition preparation and earlier identification of additional discovery needs. Brownstone anticipates changes to firms' organization and operations as research capability improves, but specifies no staffing outcome. Koh's access motivation concerns individuals unable to obtain legal help, whereas product cost-effectiveness concerns purchasers; the transcript does not demonstrate that vendor savings reach underserved people. FileRead is presented as a software vendor, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.
